rv.q: The original was so perfect that I trudged along to the Theatre Royal Haymarket full of doubts. My pessimism was ill placed. I had a blast.
In an era of international musicals, this unashamedly British night out is a change and a treat.
The comic dialogue is so delightful that it’s tempting to resent its interruption by songs that sometimes seem to have been included merely to justify the show’s title.
The result is a show that shouldn’t work and often doesn’t, but is enjoyable all the same.
This is one of too few moments where this production, entertaining as it is, finds its own feet and doesn’t simply prop itself up against the past.
In the end, I got partway there.
The crucial thing missing from this funny musical is any truly compelling reason why Del Boy and Rodney have to burst into song.
It's not half as entertaining as the original pratfall.
It's a well-meaning evening but it needs a generous audience.

Nostalgia for a dingy, down-at-heel yet somehow much-missed past runs through it, expressed brilliantly in a scene where Trigger (an undertakerish Peter Baker, an amazing match for TV’s Roger Lloyd Pack) foresees the future.

Here arrives the musical version of Only Fools and Horses, one of the BBC’s most popular sit-coms, beloved by millions, including me, and it’s a show that is as funny as the series and as dodgy as Del’s merchandise!
It has heart, wit and warmth by the bucketload.
Just how much you warm to it will largely depend on your wish to revisit a beloved TV series in this new but hardly revelatory format.
The new stage show at London’s Theatre Royal Haymarket packs in as much fun as a beano to Margate while wearing a Kiss Me Quick hat.

So as a proposition this show makes about as much sense as the mops that tell the time which Del and Rodney sell down Peckham market. And yet, a bit like Del Boy’s made-in-Uzbekistan mobile phone, this show actually works. Set in 1989, the action mostly lingers in the Trotter’s favourite boozer and their council flat.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this beloved sitcom's stage adaptation: critics praise the sharp comic dialogue and performances, but many question whether the songs justify the musical format, with some finding it unnecessary despite moments of nostalgic fun.
